concept.name: No supply
concept.definition: A price-volume indication, formalized in Tom Williams's Wyckoff-derived Volume Spread Analysis, of a deficit of sellers: typically a down-bar on narrow spread closing off its low on volume below that of the previous two bars. It indicates that selling pressure has dried up and, in the right context, that higher prices are likely; Williams also called it a 'test of supply' and favored it for long entries.
concept.intuition: The price dips but almost nobody is selling — the path of least resistance is back up.
concept.mechanics: The analyst flags narrow-spread down-bars with volume clearly below the prior two bars, then weighs the background: after a spring or during a low-volume reaction in accumulation, no-supply bars confirm supply exhaustion and support long entries. A successful test of supply is conventionally followed by an up-bar or sign of strength.
concept.failure_modes: Low-volume dips occur constantly in quiet markets and can precede renewed selling; without a bullish background (accumulation, prior spring or test), a no-supply bar has little predictive content.
concept.misconceptions: No supply does not guarantee a rally — it only shows sellers stepped back at that moment — and it is not simply any low-volume red bar; spread, close location, and context all matter.
concept.example: After a spring low, a stock drifts down on two narrow-range bars with volume at a month low and closes off the lows; the next session's wide-spread rally confirms the no-supply test and the trader buys.

citations.source: VSA and cluster analysis. No Demand and No Supply (ATAS blog, describing Tom Williams's Volume Spread Analysis)
